## Pinning does not stop at `uses:`

A pinned action can still fetch mutable content at run time. Before trusting one, read its
`action.yml` and any Dockerfile or shell script it ships, and look for:

- `uses:` references inside a composite action that are themselves on a tag or branch
- `FROM ubuntu:latest` or any unpinned base image in a Docker action
- `curl ... | bash`, `wget`, or a download from a release URL that is not checksum-verified
- `npm install`, `pip install`, or `go install` without a lockfile or a pinned version
- Network calls to a host unrelated to the action's stated purpose

Reusable workflows are third-party dependencies with the same properties. Pin
`uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/x.yml@<sha>` the same way.

OpenSSF Scorecard's Pinned-Dependencies check scores the whole repository, not only workflow
`uses:` lines. It reads Dockerfile `FROM` lines and `curl` or `wget` downloads in shipped scripts,
in addition to the workflow `uses:` lines above, and scores the fraction pinned to a hash. A full
semantic version for a Go module counts as pinned; everything else needs a digest. Package
manifests and their lock files are not part of what this check reads, but commit them for every
ecosystem that supports them regardless, since they are what makes a build reproducible. A
repository chasing that check pins its base images by `sha256` and checksum-verifies scripted
downloads, alongside the action pinning above.

## Choosing an action at all

The safest action is the one not added. A three-line `run:` step often replaces a dependency that
brings an unaudited JavaScript bundle into a job holding the repository token.

When one is warranted, check: whether the source is readable and small, whether it is actively
maintained, whether the publisher is a verified creator or a known organization, and whether the
name is a near-match for a more popular action, which is how typosquatting works. Prefer forking a
critical action into the organization and pinning that, so an upstream compromise does not propagate
automatically.

Sources read: https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-actions-workflow-lockfiles-are-generally-available/ ; https://docs.github.com/actions/concepts/security/workflow-dependency-lockfiles (linked from the changelog); and pages linked from that docs page: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/lock-workflow-dependencies , https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/administer/control-workflow-execution , https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/administer/enforce-workflow-lockfiles

(1) Locked commit must be on a branch? Yes, in the action's own repository. Docs: "This commit must be reachable from the branch or tag recorded for it in the lockfile, in the action's own repository. A commit that exists only in a fork, or that's no longer reachable from that branch or tag, is rejected when the workflow runs." So it is verified at run time, not only at generation. Generation also reports drift: a moved branch or partial ref gives a `ref-moved` warning, and `--verify` fails on a stale lockfile.

(2) Coverage:
- Reusable workflows: NOT covered. Docs: the lockfile "doesn't pin calls to reusable workflows (`jobs.<job_id>.uses`)"; reference them by full commit SHA instead. Their dependencies are covered by the lockfile of the repository where they are defined.
- Local actions: partly. The extension "never follows or locks a local path action (`uses: ./…`)". A `$/` path is pinned and its dependencies can be locked. `gh actions-lock --migrate-local-actions` rewrites `./` to `$/`. With `--ignore-local-actions`, a `./` action that uses unlocked actions fails at run time with an error such as "lockfile missing pin for ...".
- Docker actions: not mentioned on any page I read. Unknown from my sources.

(3) Run-time enforcement: Yes. "The locked commit is what runs when the workflow executes." After onboarding, "Every action dependency the workflow uses must be present in the lockfile." On mismatch (commit not reachable from the recorded ref), the run is rejected. `owner_id`/`repo_id` are also checked at run time. For a workflow not onboarded: with the Require lockfile policy Active it is blocked ("blocks runs of targeted workflows that aren't onboarded"). Without the policy the docs do not say explicitly; the gradual-onboarding wording implies it runs as before.

(4) Generate and enforce:
- Install: `gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock`
- Generate: `gh actions-lock` (all workflows) or `gh actions-lock .github/workflows/ci.yml` (one). Review the full diff, since it also rewrites uses refs (e.g. @v3 to @v3.1.0).
- Keep current: Dependabot regenerates entries only for already-onboarded workflows. CI can run `gh actions-lock --verify` as a required check.
- Enforce: set the Require lockfile policy to Active, at enterprise, organization, or repository level. Pilot first in Evaluate mode, which the enforce page says is "only available on GitHub Enterprise Cloud."
- Allowlists: once onboarded, checks use locked SHAs, so tag entries such as actions/checkout@v6 no longer match. Use a wildcard or full SHA.
- Plans: changelog says GA on "GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans."
- GHES: not mentioned on any page I read. Unknown; do not assume support.
=====
The repo states the fork-commit rule but gives no way to check it. I'm testing candidate checks against this repo's own pins and reading GitHub's changelog.
**A full-SHA pin doesn't prove the commit belongs to the repository named in `uses:`, and GitHub's commits API won't tell you either.** I asked it for the fork commit from Chainguard's post under `actions/checkout`, and for the Trivy imposter prefix `70379aad`. Both resolved.

## How it works
Forks share Git object storage with their parent, so a commit pushed to any fork can be fetched by SHA through the parent's name. `uses: actions/checkout@<fork-sha>` therefore runs attacker code that looks upstream, and passes both an `actions/*` allowlist and "require full-length SHA".

The attacker still has to **get that SHA into a workflow or tag**, through an accepted PR, stolen write access or a compromised dependency. A correct existing pin can't be redirected this way.

## The two articles
**[Chainguard](https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/what-the-fork-imposter-commits-in-github-actions-and-ci-cd) (March 2023)** is the substantive one.
- It explains the mechanism and calls it a form of dependency confusion.
- It reports no known exploitation at the time, after a non-exhaustive search.
- It offers a checker, `clank`, and notes that signing is only a partial answer.
- It predates both the 2026 incidents and lockfiles.

**[The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hackers-found-way-around-github-sha.html) (24 November 2026)** is a contributed piece promoting a webinar by a Chainguard speaker. It has no IOCs, commit SHAs, detection steps or source links.
- **The technique isn't new:** "found way around" describes something published in 2023.
- **Trivy is misleadingly compressed:** it says teams pinned to the commit "would have passed every check". Other reporting says the attacker [committed the imposter pin into Trivy's own release workflow](https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23), and separately [force-pushed 76 of 77 `trivy-action` tags](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-33634).
- **`actions-cool/issues-helper`:** I found only [one secondary mention](https://www.ajayk.sh/blog/github-actions-security-2026-supply-chain/), so treat its details as unconfirmed.

## What lockfiles change
They [became generally available on 28 October](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-actions-workflow-lockfiles-are-generally-available/), and are the first platform control here that addresses fork commits. According to the [docs](https://docs.github.com/actions/concepts/security/workflow-dependency-lockfiles), a locked commit that exists only in a fork is rejected at run time. I haven't tested that.

Limits:
- Only onboarded workflows are covered, unless the "Require lockfile" policy is active.
- Reusable workflow calls (`jobs.<id>.uses`) aren't locked.
- `./` local actions aren't locked without migrating them to `$/`.
- They don't judge whether a dependency is safe.
- The news piece says GitHub Enterprise Server isn't supported; the docs pages read didn't say.

## Checking a pin
All six distinct versioned pins in this repo's workflows match the tag in their version comment. The check for each:

```sh
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/commits/refs/tags/TAG --jq .sha   # must equal the pinned SHA
```

- **A match** shows the upstream repository's tag points there. It doesn't help if the attacker moved the tag.
- **`compare/main...SHA`** returned `diverged` for the fork commit. Legitimate release-branch commits can do the same, so it can't decide on its own.
- **`zizmor`** has an `impostor-commit` online audit, as far as I recall. I didn't test it; running `GH_TOKEN=... uvx zizmor@1.31.1 <workflow>` on a file with a known fork SHA would confirm it.

## Gaps in this repo
`skills/github/github-actions-security/references/supply-chain.md`:
1. **No verification method:** lines 34-36 say to verify the commit belongs to the repository but not how. Add the tag-match command and warn that `commits/<sha>` succeeding proves nothing.
2. **No lockfiles:** neither the pinning nor the policy section mentions them.
3. **Overstated policy control:** line 153 says required SHA pinning "makes SHA pinning an invariant". That's true, but it should add that it doesn't check where the commit came from.

I'd fix 1 and 3 now, since they're small and tested. Item 2 should be a separate change, because adopting lockfiles also affects allowlists, Dependabot and CI. I haven't edited anything.
Both fixes are in, and nothing is staged or committed.

- **`skills/github/github-actions-security/references/supply-chain.md`:**
  - Added the tag-match command for checking a pin.
  - Warned that a successful `commits/<sha>` lookup proves nothing.
  - Said that a mismatch is unresolved rather than proof of an attack, and that a match doesn't detect a moved tag.
  - Noted that required SHA pinning and allowlists don't check a commit's origin.
  - Added one checklist item.
- **`docs/controls.md`:** my edit moved a cited line, so I changed `:187` to `:202`. `--renumber` refused to run on the modified tree, so I did it by hand.

- **Passed:** `check_skills.py`, `check_capabilities.py`, `check_citations.py`, `check_content_only.py`, and `markdownlint` on the two changed files.
- **Repo-wide `markdownlint`:** it failed in the run I did, and the errors shown were all from files under `.venv/`.
- **`check_evals.py`:** it passed, with unmeasured and staleness findings that don't fail the run. I didn't re-run the paid `github-actions-security` evals, so the edited guidance is unmeasured.

## Pin to the latest release

Pinning and currency are separate requirements, and satisfying only the first produces the worst
outcome: an action frozen at a version whose known vulnerabilities are never fixed, with the pin
providing the appearance of control. A SHA pin is not a reason to stay on an old version; it is the
reason updating has to be deliberate.

Whenever a `uses:` line is added or touched, resolve the action's current release rather than
carrying the version already in the file forward:
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
```

- Dependabot updates SHA pins and rewrites the version comment, so pinning does not freeze a
  repository at an old version. It is what keeps the latest-release rule true between changes, rather
  than only at the moment someone edits the file, so configure it in any repository that pins.
- A cooldown, `cooldown` for Dependabot or `minimumReleaseAge` for Renovate, delays adoption of a
  brand-new release. Most malicious releases are found and yanked within days, so a delay of about a
  week absorbs a large share of the risk at little cost.
- Security alerts for actions are generated from semantic versions. A SHA-pinned action receives
  version-update pull requests but may not raise an alert, so the update pull requests must actually
  be reviewed and merged rather than left open.
- Review a Dependabot action bump by reading the upstream diff between the two SHAs, not by trusting
  the version number.

## Policy enforcement

Set these at the organization or enterprise level, in Settings, Actions, Policies. They apply to
every repository regardless of what a workflow file says:

- **Allowed actions.** Choose the most restrictive level the organization can work with: enterprise
  actions only; enterprise plus verified creators; or an explicit allowlist. Entries prefixed with
  `!` block an action or version, and the blocklist is evaluated last, overriding any allow rule.
- **Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA.** Available since August 2025 as a
  checkbox alongside the allowed-actions policy. Workflows referencing an unpinned action fail
  validation. This is the control that makes SHA pinning an invariant rather than a review comment.
  It checks the form of the reference, not its origin, so an imposter commit passes it, and passes an
  allowlist entry for the repository it imitates.
- Keep the policy in version control and apply it through the API, so changes are auditable and can
  be reverted quickly during an incident.

## Cache and artifact poisoning

Caches are shared across a repository, and a pull request from a branch can write a cache entry that
a later privileged run on the default branch restores.

- **Disable caching in release and publishing workflows.** A poisoned cache entry restored into a
  release build is a direct path into the published artifact. This includes the implicit caching in
  setup actions, such as `actions/setup-node` with `cache: npm`.
- Do not cache anything derived from a pull request build into a key that a default-branch run will
  match.
- Treat an artifact downloaded from another workflow run as untrusted input. See
  [untrusted-input.md](untrusted-input.md) for the `workflow_run` rules.

## Provenance

For anything published to consumers, generate an attestation in the same job that produced the
artifact:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
  attestations: write

steps:
  - uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@<full-sha> # v4.x
    with:
      subject-path: dist/*.tar.gz
```

Verify with `gh attestation verify <file> --repo <owner>/<repo>`. An attestation is only meaningful
if consumers verify it, so document the verification command alongside the release.

Attaching the provenance file (`*.intoto.jsonl`) to the GitHub release also satisfies the top tier
of OpenSSF Scorecard's Signed-Releases check, which reads release assets for a signature or a SLSA
provenance file on each of the last five releases.

- [ ] Every `uses:` reference pinned to a full 40-character SHA with a version comment
- [ ] The SHA was resolved from the source repository, not written from memory
- [ ] Each new or changed SHA matches the release tag in its version comment
- [ ] Each version is the newest release that clears the cooldown, looked up during this change, or

- [ ] Release notes read for every version skipped by an upgrade, with major-version implications

- [ ] Composite actions, Docker base images, and install scripts inside a pinned action checked for

- [ ] New actions justified: readable source, maintained, correct name, minimal alternative
      considered
- [ ] Dependabot configured for `github-actions` with a cooldown, and its pull requests reviewed
      against the upstream diff
- [ ] Organization policy restricts allowed actions and requires SHA pinning
- [ ] No caching in release or publishing workflows, including implicit setup-action caches

gh api orgs/ORG/actions/permissions/selected-actions

- Require approval for workflows from all outside contributors rather than only first-time ones. A
